Operation

Phylogenetic inference

Reconstruct the evolutionary relationships among samples from an alignment.

Inputs

  • Whole-genome alignment (optionally masked or filtered)
  • Collection dates (method-dependent)

Outputs

  • Phylogenetic tree (Newick)
  • Time-scaled tree (method-dependent)

The resulting tree is the main product for interpreting population structure, identifying clusters, and placing new samples in context. More than one method can be applied in sequence, so a tree from one method can be the starting point for another.

Choosing methods 3

These methods address different problems and can be combined. Apply each one whose conditions match your data.

  • Bayesian phylogeny

    Jointly estimate a time-scaled tree, molecular clock, and population model, with uncertainty on every estimate.

    Use when

    • You need credible intervals on dates, such as when a lineage was introduced.
    • You want phylodynamic estimates, such as population growth, reproduction numbers, or migration between locations.
    • The dataset is small enough to run in reasonable time, typically hundreds to a few thousand short genomes, or a subsample of a larger collection.

    Skip this method when

    • The dataset is large or results are needed routinely and quickly. Use Time-scaled phylogeny instead.
    • Dates are missing or there is little temporal signal. Use Maximum likelihood phylogeny instead.

    BEAST X · BEAST 2

  • Maximum likelihood phylogeny

    Find the tree that best explains the alignment under a substitution model, with branch lengths in substitutions per site.

    Use when

    • You need a tree for clustering, population structure, or placing new samples. This is the default choice.
    • Collection dates are missing or unreliable.
    • You want a fast result with branch support values, even for thousands of genomes.

    Combine with

    • Time-scaled phylogeny: Apply it afterward to convert this tree's branch lengths into time when collection dates are available.

    IQ-TREE · RAxML-NG

  • Time-scaled phylogeny

    Rescale an existing tree, usually a maximum likelihood tree, so branch lengths are in time and ancestral nodes are dated.

    Use when

    • You need dates for events, such as introductions, common ancestors, or transmission windows.
    • You already have a tree, such as a maximum likelihood tree, and accurate collection dates for most samples.
    • The dataset is too large for a full Bayesian analysis, or results are needed quickly.

    Skip this method when

    • Dates are missing or imprecise, or a root-to-tip regression shows little temporal signal.
    • Samples were collected over a period too short for measurable evolution, so dates would be poorly constrained.
    • You need full uncertainty on the tree and dates, or phylodynamic estimates such as growth rates. Use Bayesian phylogeny instead.

    Combine with

    • Maximum likelihood phylogeny: Build the maximum likelihood tree first; this method takes it as input.

    TreeTime · LSD2 (in IQ-TREE)
